meta.title: Comparative Politics knowledge network, c. 1959-2026
meta.description: Key works and debates in comparative politics: democratization and backsliding, authoritarian institutions and information control, Chinese politics, state capacity and development, redistribution and political economy, parties, populism, clientelism, ethnicity, contention, corruption, gender and institutional theory. Seeds come from this repo's papers.json; works shared with the other maps are imported from them; others are top-cited 2006-2026 articles selected via Crossref plus anchoring classics. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work).

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works come from the user's Zotero library. Works shared with the IPE, security and IR maps keep their earlier verification. Crossref-selected works take title, authors, year, venue and DOI from Crossref records. All new anchors were found in Crossref (books often via reviews, chapters or reprint DOIs). One-line claims for non-repo works are my summaries.

Inequality and asset mobility as the mechanism.

Rising middle classes demand democracy to protect property.
Income predicts transitions with a three-category regime coding.

International linkage and leverage shape regime change.

Measurement uncertainty matters for regime findings.
Backsliding replaces transitions as the main dynamic.
Experimental test that partisans trade democracy for policy.
Partisanship, not declining values, drives tolerance of violations.
Declining democratic support after the crisis.
Measures affective polarization across European party systems, the condition Svolik argues weakens voters' defense of democracy.
Argues that women's growing presence in politics, spurred by quotas, has provoked violence meant to push them out.
Power sharing breaks down as dictators accumulate power.
Power sharing and control as authoritarianism's two problems.
Legislatures constrain rulers and raise investment.

Hybrid regime leaders face economic accountability.
Military power and moral hazard in dictatorships.
External commitments as substitutes for domestic institutions.
Encompassing interests and credible property rights.
Contentious politics builds states and durable autocracies.
Revolutions are unpredictable due to preference falsification.

Strategic tolerance of information for monitoring.

Technology can lower the costs of coordinated opposition.

Concealment of grievances in upward reporting.
Factional ties, not growth, explain elite promotion.
Performance matters at lower levels only.
Informal institutions for accountability in rural China.
Uses large-scale online data, as in King, Pan and Roberts, to map the ideological divisions of Chinese citizens.
Kinship geography, not war, shapes state building in imperial China.
FDI empowers subnational leaders in Vietnam.
Without interstate war, African states stayed weak.
Legacies of historical conflict in Africa.
Missionaries, not settler institutions, explain much of democracy.
Strong property rights can undermine development.
Redistribution takes inefficient forms to preserve power.
Winners of partial reform capture the state.
Deliberation, not regime type, stabilizes growth.
Democracy does not make the poor better off.
Governance indicators are contaminated by growth.
Autocratic growth reflects selection, not regime advantage.
Insurance motives reverse the inequality effect.
Electoral institutions shape redistribution via coalitions.
National identity lowers demand for redistribution.
The skew of inequality, not its level, drives redistribution.
War, not democratization, produced progressive taxation.
Openness enlarges government only in democracies.
Power resources, not employer interests, built welfare states.
Dependent market economies in Eastern Europe.
New politics of the welfare state.
Class voting in a tripolar space.
Electoral and party systems within patterns of democracy.
Low-magnitude PR balances representation and accountability.
Consensus versus majoritarian patterns, not veto-player counts, explain performance.
Shows post-communist party systems stay highly volatile, mostly through party entry and exit, complementing evidence of weak party anchoring in Europe.
Ethnic nationalism among radical right voters.
Demand and supply of far right success.
Contextual drivers of extreme right voting.
Reviews far-right parties, including their limited policy effects.
Radical right success shifts mainstream positions.
Populism and technocracy as rivals to party government.
Cultural backlash as the driver of populism.
Cultural backlash, not economic shocks, drives populist voting.
Economic roots of left and right populism.
Experimental evidence within the patrons-and-clients framework.
Coethnic sanctioning explains public goods failure.
Opportunity structures cannot predict sudden revolutions.
Institutions create trust, not civic traditions.
Coercive apparatus decides outcomes of uprisings.
Tests how regime type shapes repression, drawing on the repression-dissent framework surveyed in his review.
Victimization, not only civic culture, drives participation.
Impartiality, not a list of causes, is the core of quality of government.
Corruption and trust reinforce each other.
Movements, not descriptive representation, drive policy.
Growth in women's representation depends on more than oil.
Offers a data-driven way to choose comparison units, a formal counterpart to the controlled case comparison.
Ideas and discourse as sources of change.
Gradual institutional change, including in weak institutions.
Global coup data underpin the analysis of protest and coup coordination.
Argues the conditions that sustain an existing democracy differ from those that create it, contesting functional prerequisites and offering a phase-based model driven by elite decisions.
Develops Rustow's elite-centred genetic model of transition into a theory of pacts and splits between regime hardliners and softliners.
Recasts Moore's landed-elite thesis: old-regime elites need not block democracy if a strong conservative party lets them win under open competition.
Generalizes the historical claim that robust conservative parties act as gatekeepers against extremists into a diagnosis of contemporary democratic breakdown.
Finds most democratizations stem from incumbent errors rather than deliberate concessions by elites seeking to forestall revolution.
Shows that many of O'Donnell and Schmitter's liberalizing softliners were autocrats who miscalculated rather than leaders who intended to democratize.
Shows income protects democracies from coups and incumbent takeovers chiefly by marking which democracies are consolidated, refining the Przeworski-Limongi survival finding.
Uses the distinction between military coups and incumbent takeovers to document the shift from open coups toward executive aggrandizement.
Supplies the formal model behind the claim that polarized voters trade democratic principles for partisan interests.
Locates the threat to democracy in polarization that makes voters tolerate partisan abuses, not in a secular decline of citizens' commitment to democracy.
Tests with a 135-country panel whether mass support for democracy sustains it, finding support predicts later democratic survival.
Finds democratic support falls after democratic gains and rises after backsliding, so falling support is not evidence of secular deconsolidation.
Complements the finding that support sustains democracy by showing that changes in democracy also feed back into support.
Extends the voter-tolerance logic with reference-dependent preferences, so each small violation resets expectations and escapes punishment.
Formalizes why contemporary backsliding takes the incremental executive-aggrandizement form Bermeo describes rather than abrupt coups.
Models the incremental executive aggrandizement Haggard and Kaufman trace, showing concealment of the endpoint lets incumbents dismantle checks voters would reject wholesale.
Formalizes subversion by stealth, specifying when voters fail to stop an incumbent before democratic checks are gone.
Builds on Wintrobe's view that dictators must purchase loyalty as well as repress, treating nominally democratic institutions as devices for co-opting opponents.
Starts from Wintrobe's loyalty-repression trade-off to analyze the separate problems of authoritarian power-sharing and control.
Applies North and Weingast's credible-commitment logic to the autocrat's own supporters, who need institutions to punish a ruler who reneges.
Models when authoritarian institutions make power-sharing credible, formalizing Myerson's claim that autocrats need institutions to bind themselves to supporters.
Attributes ruling-party cohesion to shared origins in violent struggle, not to patronage or credible power-sharing arrangements, which tend to fail in crises.
Revives Huntington's link between revolutionary origins and strong institutionalized parties to explain authoritarian durability.
Tests whether authoritarian legislatures serve co-optation and information functions using query sessions in Vietnam's National Assembly.
Builds on evidence from Vietnam that authoritarian deputies relay constituent concerns to argue Chinese consultative institutions channel information to the regime.
Formalizes the revelation of hidden anti-regime preferences as an informational cascade driven by observed protest turnout in Leipzig.
Finds outside information via West German TV made East Germans more satisfied with the regime, contrary to the view that information flows fuel mobilization against autocracy.
Like Kern and Hainmueller, finds media exposure can stabilize authoritarian rule, here because marketized Chinese media appear credible while staying within party limits.
Argues propaganda works by signalling regime strength rather than by persuasion, so exposure breeds fear of the state rather than approval.
Generalizes the finding of porous, selective censorship into a theory of fear, friction and flooding that steers most citizens away from sensitive information.
Generalizes the logic of information-tolerant dictators into informational autocrats who maintain a reputation for competence through manipulation rather than mass repression.
Tests a core tactic of informational autocracy: Russian state TV blames foreign actors for bad economic news and credits the Kremlin for good news.
Formalizes the cadre-evaluation incentives O'Brien and Li identified, showing personnel control tied to measurable targets drives local officials' behavior.
Extends the finding that cadres prioritize hard measurable targets to show how target-based evaluation produces manipulated statistics.
Shows representative assemblies constrained rulers and secured credit mainly in compact polities where representatives could meet often and monitor the executive.
Finds European territorial states formed where prosperity let local elites fund independent rule, and that war did not systematically eliminate small states.
Generalizes self-enforcing limits on the sovereign into a coordination model in which citizens jointly police state transgressions.
Treats Weingast's coordination account as a foundational explanation of how limits on government become self-enforcing when reviewing the rule of law and development.
Shows African democracies abolished visible school fees but did not improve hard-to-monitor inputs, specifying when democracy does and does not help the poor.
Tests the rentier, repression and modernization mechanisms catalogued in the review of resource-curse explanations.
Integrates Karl's account of how oil booms shape petro-state institutions with cognitive and societal explanations of the resource curse.
Argues resource rents can promote democracy where non-resource inequality is high, because rents reduce elites' fear of redistribution.
Folds the oil-and-women argument into a broader account of how the size, secrecy and volatility of petroleum revenues shape regimes, gender and conflict.
Defends the oil-authoritarianism link against Haber and Menaldo's long-run reappraisal, arguing the curse emerged after the 1970s nationalizations.
Tests the taxation-representation mechanism behind rentier theory, finding taxes relative to services, not tax levels, predict democratization.
Field experiment shows citizens told spending is tax-financed rather than windfall-financed monitor and sanction government more, micro evidence on why rents weaken accountability.
Treats oil production as endogenous to prior industrialization and finds no anti-democratic effect once that endogeneity is modelled.
Reinforces Haber and Menaldo's skepticism about the political resource curse with a different identification strategy.
Draws on evidence that PR systems foster contagion of women candidates when modelling the growth of women's legislative representation over time.
Finds parties adopt gender quotas partly through contagion after rivals do, extending the contagion mechanism from nominations to formal rules.
Moves from party-level quota adoption to the global spread of national quotas and their effects.
Tests the role-model effect of descriptive representation, finding girls and women are more politically engaged where female MPs are more visible.
Uses randomized reservation of village council leadership for women in India to show women leaders invest in goods women prefer.
Extends the finding that women leaders shift spending toward women's priorities from Indian villages to national quotas and budgets worldwide.
Builds on evidence that corruption victimization erodes regime legitimacy, modelling corruption and trust as mutually reinforcing in Mexico.
Shows voters punished malfeasant Italian deputies only once press coverage expanded, a condition on when corruption information produces accountability.
Starts from evidence that released audits lower corrupt incumbents' vote shares and asks when citizens find such information credible.
Derives social-policy preferences from skill specificity, supplying the micro-foundation linking coordinated market economies to generous social insurance.
Replaces skill specificity with occupational unemployment risk as the micro-level driver of demand for redistribution.
Shows that when spending is insurance rather than pure redistribution, greater inequality lowers the median voter's demand for spending.
Tests the insurance model on disaggregated spending, finding inequality reduces insurance-type welfare spending.
Defends power-resources theory against employer-centred accounts, arguing employers consented to welfare reforms rather than being their protagonists.
Applies strategic-coordination logic to the choice of electoral rules, explaining switches to PR by threatened ruling parties.
Expands the typology of programmatic versus clientelistic linkages into a comparative research program on democratic accountability.
Explains the prevalence of clientelistic linkages in young democracies by politicians' inability to make credible programmatic promises.
Adds a vanguard whose violence signals regime weakness, showing how entrepreneurs shift thresholds in preference-falsification models of revolution.
Generalizes the consociational model of elite accommodation in segmented societies into the broader consensus-democracy type.
Replaces supply-side institutional complementarities with demand-side growth models to explain divergence among advanced economies after the 1990s.
